# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease [1]. First described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the phenomenon was initially regarded as an angiographic curiosity but has since been recognized as a clinically relevant cause of chest pain and recurrent hospitalization [2]. CSFP predominantly affects young male smokers and may account for a meaningful proportion of patients undergoing angiography for chest pain who are found to have angiographically "normal" coronary arteries [3].

## Definition and Quantification

CSFP is most reliably diagnosed using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count, a reproducible quantitative method introduced by Gibson and colleagues that counts the number of cineangiographic frames required for contrast to reach standardized distal coronary landmarks [4]. A corrected TIMI frame count exceeding two standard deviations above the established normal mean is generally used to define slow flow [5]. The TIMI frame count has facilitated standardization across studies and remains the cornerstone of objective diagnosis [6].

## Pathophysiology

The pathophysiological basis of CSFP remains incompletely understood, but several overlapping mechanisms have been proposed. Microvascular dysfunction is widely regarded as central, with abnormal coronary microvascular resistance demonstrated in affected patients [7]. Histopathological studies of myocardial biopsies have revealed microvascular abnormalities including endothelial swelling, thickening of the capillary basement membrane, and luminal narrowing of small vessels [8]. Endothelial dysfunction has been consistently implicated, evidenced by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilatation [9, 10].

Subclinical atherosclerosis is another contributing factor; intravascular ultrasound studies have shown diffuse intimal thickening and calcification even in segments appearing normal on angiography [11]. Inflammation also plays a role, with elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and other inflammatory markers reported in CSFP patients [12, 13]. Increased oxidative stress and reduced antioxidant capacity have likewise been documented [14]. Some investigators have proposed that platelet dysfunction and a prothrombotic milieu contribute, supported by altered mean platelet volume and platelet activation indices [15].

## Clinical Associations and Risk Factors

CSFP is strongly associated with traditional cardiovascular risk factors, particularly cigarette smoking, male sex, obesity, and components of the metabolic syndrome [16, 17]. Insulin resistance and abnormal glucose metabolism have been linked to the phenomenon [18]. Associations with hyperuricemia and dyslipidemia have also been reported [19]. The clinical relevance lies in the recurrent and sometimes disabling angina experienced by these patients, which may persist despite reassurance regarding the absence of obstructive disease [20].

## Clinical Presentation and Outcomes

The most common presentation is recurrent chest pain, which may be either typical or atypical, and a substantial proportion of patients present with acute coronary syndromes [21]. CSFP has been associated with electrocardiographic abnormalities, including QT dispersion, fragmented QRS, and a predisposition to ventricular and atrial arrhythmias [22, 23]. Cases of life-threatening arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, though uncommon, have been reported, underscoring that CSFP is not entirely benign [24]. Impaired left ventricular diastolic function and reduced functional capacity have also been demonstrated [25]. Overall, long-term prognosis is generally favorable, but quality of life is frequently impaired by persistent symptoms and repeated healthcare utilization [26].

## Management

There is no universally accepted treatment for CSFP, and management remains largely empirical. Dipyridamole and other agents that improve microvascular function have been investigated with variable success [27]. Calcium channel blockers, particularly mibefradil and diltiazem, have shown benefit in reducing the TIMI frame count and relieving angina [28]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric oxide–potentiating properties, and statins, which improve endothelial function and reduce inflammation, have shown promise in small trials [29]. Aggressive modification of risk factors—especially smoking cessation, weight reduction, and glycemic control—is recommended as a foundational component of care [30].

## Conclusion

The coronary slow flow phenomenon is an increasingly recognized clinical entity that bridges microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, subclinical atherosclerosis, and inflammation. Although generally associated with a favorable long-term prognosis, it can cause substantial morbidity through recurrent angina and, rarely, serious arrhythmic events. The TIMI frame count provides a reproducible diagnostic tool, but standardized treatment strategies are lacking. Future research employing larger randomized trials and advanced imaging of the coronary microvasculature is needed to clarify pathogenesis and define evidence-based therapy.
